[MUQATIL:18:32-33/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The likeness is a description for the people of Mecca; mathal means a likeness.
[MUQATIL:18:32-33/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The two brothers were Israelites: the believer was Yamlīkha, the unbeliever Firtas, and each inherited four thousand dinars from their father.
[MUQATIL:18:32-33/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The believer spent his inheritance on the poor, orphans, and needy; the unbeliever invested in houses, livestock, and gardens.
[MUQATIL:18:32-33/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The unbelieving brother is the one given two gardens.

[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلوحمارقبل|فالواوأشركتبينهمافىالباءفجريا#202/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أَوْ coordinates alternatives, asserting passage for one rather than both; a denial of both is phrased ما مررت بواحد منهما, while denying one names that one.

[TAB-FULL:v1p35/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | At Adhāt Banī Ghifār, Gabriel successively conveyed commands to recite on one, two, three, then seven aḥruf; the Prophet sought relief for his community, and said any of the seven is correct.
[TAB-FULL:v1p35/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبي بن كعب | reports | Ubayy heard two men recite Sūrat al-Naḥl differently; each said the Prophet had taught him his reading.
[TAB-FULL:v1p35/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet asked each man to recite and affirmed both readings as good, calming Ubayy's distress at the differences.
[TAB-FULL:v1p35/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | When Ubayy reddened with demonic misgivings, the Prophet touched his chest and prayed for Satan to be driven away from him.
[TAB-FULL:v1p35/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says God granted seven aḥruf and a request with each successive command; he asked forgiveness for his community and reserved his third intercession for Judgment Day.
[TAB-FULL:v1p37/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet accepted two men’s differing recitations, then Ubayy’s, affirming each as correct after they said he had taught it.
[TAB-FULL:v1p37/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبي | reports | Ubayy recounts that permission expanded from one letter to seven after repeated requests for ease; each reading carried a supplication, with a final intercession reserved for his community.
[TAB-FULL:v1p37/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Bakra reports Gabriel asked for one letter and Michael for more, until six or seven; all suffice provided mercy and punishment verses are not exchanged, like come and approach.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p283/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | The Meccan polytheists, advised by Jews, asked Muhammad about the Cave Companions, the Spirit, and the two men; God made the parable an example for the Prophet, unbelievers, believers, and deniers.

[NAHHAS:v2p455/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The underlying construction is ‘an example, the likeness of two men.’
[KHATTABI:v1p62/r1] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | holds | The opening of al-Nābigha’s poem is exceptionally beautiful and eloquently conveys distress and a long, sleepless night; it was said no poet began better.
[KHATTABI:v1p62/r2] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | holds | The image of a chest relieved by night borrows from a shepherd settling camels at their nighttime resting place; its natural ease joins eloquence and sweetness.
[KHATTABI:v1p62/r3] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | prefers | Al-Nābigha’s lines are accomplished, but al-Imruʾ al-Qays surpasses them in crafted technique, simile, and inventive meanings.
[KHATTABI:v1p62/r4] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | holds | Al-Imruʾ al-Qays gives night a body and compares gathering darkness to successive, colliding sea waves.
[KHATTABI:v1p62/r5] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | holds | He depicts the stars as firmly rope-bound, motionless, and unable to depart, intensifying the night’s oppressive stillness.
[KHATTABI:v1p62/r6] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | holds | The poem first longs for dawn as relief, then reverses course: the affliction is too great for any time to end or cure it.
[KHATTABI:v1p62/r7] KHATTABI, d. 388 · الشعبي | reports | The report says al-Walīd stamped his foot while hearing the poem, and al-Shaʿbī declared the matter settled, signaling recognition of al-Imruʾ al-Qays’s excellence.
[KHATTABI:v1p62/r8] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | holds | A comparison of competing poems distinguishes their levels by deciding whether one leads, the other falls short, or they are equal.
[KHATTABI:v1p63/r1] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | holds | When poets share a subject, one can reach its summit while the other falls short; al-Aʿshā’s treatment of wine outdoes al-Akhṭal’s.
[KHATTABI:v1p63/r2] KHATTABI, d. 388 · هشام ابن أدهم المازني | reports | Hishām reports that al-Shaʿbī visited a drunken al-Akhṭal, who boasted of his wine verse; al-Shaʿbī preferred al-Aʿshā’s verse, and al-Akhṭal conceded.
[KHATTABI:v1p63/r3] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | prefers | Al-Akhṭal says the wine’s aroma reaches a person with a cold, whereas al-Aʿshā makes its sharp aroma dispel congestion and cure the ailment, a stronger image.
[KHATTABI:v1p63/r4] KHATTABI, d. 388 · author | holds | A more striking form of poetic contest builds something up and then demolishes it, or establishes an idea before reversing it.
[KHATTABI:v1p63/r5] KHATTABI, d. 388 · حسان بن ثابت | reports | Jabala asked Ḥassān to disparage wine because it had captivated him; Ḥassān began a verse saying the cup would otherwise be worth nothing to its drinker.
[BAQILLANI:v1p294/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | Opponents wrongly explain the Qurʾān’s inimitability as the Messenger’s privileged knowledge of composition, which others lack; on that account they cannot distinguish divine from prophetic authorship.
[BAQILLANI:v1p294/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Bāqillānī locates the obstacle in inability to produce Qurʾānic composition, not merely in lacking knowledge of how it is composed.
[BAQILLANI:v1p294/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Knowing a craft’s rules does not ensure equal performance: people may know meters, eloquence, weaving, or archery yet differ in natural ability and execution.
[BAQILLANI:v1p294/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | One exceptional line better than Imruʾ al-Qays does not prove its poet knows composition better; if knowledge were decisive, the poet’s whole body of work would match that level.
[BAQILLANI:v1p294/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | A person may know how to write yet be unable to reproduce an existing line exactly, showing that knowledge can remain while capacity fails.
[THALABI:v6p169/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The syntax makes ‘two men’ the object, with an implied comparison: ‘set out for them a parable like two men.’

[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p173/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A generic red rose is an inadequate counterpart when the intended flower has white around its red center; the compared image must share that defining condition.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p173/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In a multi-part simile, one comparison may be placed as a dependent description of the other instead of being coordinated with it, as in the line about gray hair rising in youth.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p173/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | When waw introduces a circumstantial clause, that clause remains subordinate like an adjective; the Mars-and-Jupiter example makes the second image dependent on the first.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p173/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Stars falling are grammatically a description of night, so they remain subordinate; likewise the night is described as having day call at its sides.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p173/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Imru al-Qays's paired dates are an exception: the two items are coordinated on both sides, and a plural such as 'hearts' does not make one item subordinate to another.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p173/r6] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In the Imru al-Qays example the explicit coordination is in the predicate, 'fresh and dry'; the plural form on the subject similarly encompasses distinct equal items.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p173/r7] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The line about the speaker adorning a company with praise compares only the act of praise to hanging a pearl on a pig: praise is wasted on those unable to benefit from adornment.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p173/r8] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | That comparison concerns the whole act with its complement, not hanging by itself; waw means 'with' because there are no two parallel predicates to coordinate.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p175/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Unlike fa, thumma, and aw, wāw adds no sequence, delay, or alternative; it only joins elements under the grammatical relation they share.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p175/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Coordinated clauses need a meaningful relation: saying Zayd stands and ʿAmr sits presumes that ʿAmr is connected to Zayd and that the listener cares to learn his state too.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p175/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Joining a clause unrelated to its predecessor makes the sentence absurd, as in the example of leaving home and then praising a poet with no connection.
